learn.canDo: Choose range, hash, compound, or directory sharding for a workload and say which queries stay on one shard.
learn.why: The sharding scheme decides whether writes spread and which queries are cheap. Naming the hot tail of a time-ordered range is a standard design-review catch.
learn.keyIdea: Ranges keep neighbours together; hashes spread them.

learn.canDo: Pick a shard key from the main access paths and serve a second path with a copy, counting the write cost.
learn.why: The shard key is the hardest decision to undo. Interviewers listen for whether you start from the queries or from the data.
learn.keyIdea: The key chooses which query is cheap.

learn.canDo: Work out how overloaded a shard gets from one hot key, and relieve it with a cache and salting.
learn.why: Celebrity keys overload a single shard while the cluster looks healthy. Knowing that more shards will not help is the first step.
learn.keyIdea: More shards spread keys, not one key.

learn.canDo: Explain why hash mod N reshuffles everything, and use a ring with virtual nodes so only about 1 in N+1 keys move.
learn.why: Consistent hashing is one of the most-asked distributed systems topics, and the virtual node follow-up separates memorised answers from understood ones.
learn.keyIdea: Only the new node's arc moves.

learn.canDo: Estimate how much data a rebalance moves and pick a throttle that balances duration against user-visible latency.
learn.why: Adding nodes under load is where sharded systems hurt. The honest answer names the amount moved, the time it takes, and the cost to users.
learn.keyIdea: Rebalancing is a tax on live traffic.

chapter.story: Pigeon's data no longer fits on one machine, and the team has to decide which rows live where.
outcomes: Choose a sharding scheme and shard key from the access paths
Add nodes with a consistent hashing ring and virtual nodes
chapter.why: Splitting data is the first step that cannot be undone cheaply. The key you choose decides what is fast, what fans out, and where the hot spots appear.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can shard a table, justify the key, and say what happens when a node is added or a celebrity appears. At work you will spot a hot partition from a graph.
